name: The Zero-Sum Game
statement: One player's gain is exactly the other's loss, so the pie is fixed.
meaning: A zero-sum game is a situation in which one participant's gain is exactly balanced by an equivalent loss to the others, so the total of all payoffs is zero for every outcome. It is a strictly competitive interaction over a fixed quantity: whatever one side wins, the other loses by the same amount, and there is no way for all parties to come out ahead together.
mechanism: Payoffs across all players sum to a constant — zero — in every outcome, the special case of a constant-sum game where the constant is zero. Because the total is fixed, cooperation cannot expand the joint payoff; one player can be made better off only by making another worse off. In the two-player case the game is captured by a single payoff matrix, since one player's gain is the other's loss, which is exactly what makes such games so tractable and solvable by the minimax theorem.

examples.text: Two players each show a coin; one wins if they match, the other if they differ, so every outcome is a pure transfer between them — the canonical two-player zero-sum game.
The money one player wins equals what the others lose, so the pot is merely redistributed — though the house's cut makes real casino play negative-sum for the players collectively.
Chess and other strictly competitive board games and matches are zero-sum: one side's win is the other's loss, with no way for both to gain.

variants.name: Non-zero-sum games
variants.text: The far larger class in which one player's gain need not equal another's loss, so mutual gain is possible — as when two countries trade surpluses and both benefit.

variants.name: Zero-sum thinking
variants.text: The cognitive bias of treating a situation as fixed-pie competition when it is not, applying win-lose logic to interactions where cooperation could make everyone better off.

whyItMatters: It is a foundational concept in game theory and the setting for von Neumann's minimax theorem, defining the class of purely competitive interactions. Just as important is knowing its boundary: recognising that most real interactions — trade, growth, cooperation — are not zero-sum, and that treating them as if they were is a well-documented and costly error.

working.lead: Check whether the pie is fixed
working.text: before treating a situation as win-lose, ask whether the total really is fixed, since most interactions allow mutual gain.
for a genuine two-player zero-sum game, find the optimal play through the minimax theorem and its value.
resist the bias of casting positive-sum situations like trade or negotiation as pure competition, which leads to worse outcomes.

limits: Zero-sum games are a narrow, idealised class; most real-world interactions are not zero-sum. Trade, investment, innovation, and economic growth are positive-sum, expanding the total, while some interactions, such as costly wars and litigation, are negative-sum, shrinking it. Treating positive-sum situations as zero-sum is a recognised cognitive bias with real consequences, from misjudged negotiations to zero-sum framings of trade and immigration. Even the standard examples carry caveats: poker is zero-sum only among the players before the house takes its cut.
misreadings: It is not a description of how most of the world works — most interactions are positive-sum, allowing all parties to gain, and treating them as zero-sum is a documented fallacy. And 'zero-sum' as a worldview is a contested metaphor, quite distinct from the precise mathematical class of games.
origin: Formalised in John von Neumann's 1928 paper 'Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele,' where he proved the minimax theorem for two-person zero-sum games; developed further in von Neumann and Morgenstern's Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944).

sources.text: Zero-sum game, Wikipedia. — the fixed-total definition, the contrast with non-zero-sum games, and the zero-sum-thinking fallacy.
Minimax theorem, Wikipedia. — von Neumann's 1928 result for two-person zero-sum games.
